paras: The lynching of Charles Marshall was the hanging of a former livery-stable hand by a band of armed men at Belleville, Esmeralda County, Nevada, in early December 1880. Marshall was accused of killing John (Jack) McCann, an older man who had replaced him at the stable, and was seized and hanged before any trial. A brief wire dispatch carried the story across the country, while Nevada papers printed fuller local accounts that contradicted the wire on how Marshall was taken.

Marshall, about thirty years old, had worked as a roustabout in Gildersleeve's livery stable and was described as a "Texas cow-boy" who "prided himself on being a desperado." He was discharged after a drinking spree and McCann, a man of nearly sixty, was hired in his place. According to the Esmeralda Herald's correspondent, Marshall, drunk again, shot McCann at close range in the stable on the night of December 7 and then stamped and kicked him to death. The Virginia Chronicle's informant instead placed the killing at about 5 A.M. on Wednesday and said Marshall beat McCann's head with his pistol before walking to the Belleville Hotel for breakfast.

The Herald credited two strangers sleeping in the stable with reporting the killing, which led to Marshall's arrest the next morning and a coroner's inquest on McCann. The Chronicle named a single witness, a Fish Lake Valley teamster called Winterson, who told a friend, and said the information went to the Vigilance Committee.

In the Herald's account, Sheriff Clem Ogg placed the ironed prisoner in the charge of a guard, J. S. Longabaugh, for the night. At about 4 A.M. eight masked and heavily armed men came to the door, made Longabaugh stand aside at pistol point, and gagged and pinioned Marshall. They took him to the rear of Farrington's blacksmith shop and hanged him from a frame, with "quite a number outside" helping, and the sheriff, called from bed, "retired again and said nothing."

The Chronicle's version had eight men enter Marshall's room in the Belleville Hotel at 3 A.M. on Thursday, make him dress, and hang him from a crossbeam near the principal blacksmith shop. Marshall said nothing when asked for a last statement. His body was cut down about three hours later, carted outside the town limits and buried without a coffin in a hole behind the slaughterhouse.

According to the Chronicle's informant, opinion in Esmeralda County was "almost unanimous" in support of the Vigilance Committee, whose members were "well-known, respectable citizens." No report of an inquest on Marshall, a grand jury inquiry or any arrest of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

The first report was a Belleville dispatch of December 10, relayed through San Francisco, which said citizens rushed the sheriff and his posse as they started for the county seat at Aurora and hanged Marshall on the outskirts of town. Papers from New York and Portland, Maine, to Chicago ran it on December 11 under headlines such as "LYNCHING A MURDERER" and "A Murderer Lynched," calling Marshall "a noted desperado" and McCann "an inoffensive old man." Condensed versions appeared in weekly crime columns in Wisconsin, Delaware, Ohio and Minnesota through mid-December, with the Minnesota item garbling Marshall into "a noted deserter of Tennessee."

Nevada papers followed with longer accounts: the Gold Hill Daily News and Eureka Daily Sentinel reprinted the Esmeralda Herald's letter, and the Silver State printed the Virginia Chronicle's report. The Daily Los Angeles Herald carried the Chronicle report on December 19, including a section headed "THE LYNCHING APPROVED." No paper in the coverage gave Marshall's race or framed the killing in racial terms.

The accounts disagree on whether Marshall was in custody: the wire had him taken from the sheriff's posse, the Herald from a guard, and the Chronicle from his own hotel room. The Chronicle called the sheriff-and-posse story "incorrect" and suggested it began because Sheriff Ogg was a proprietor of the hotel where Marshall stayed. The date also varies, with the dispatch placing the hanging on Friday, December 10, and the Chronicle on Thursday morning, December 9.

reader.title: Lynching of Charles Marshall
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Every account has Marshall, accused of murdering John (Jack) McCann, seized by a party of citizens or eight armed men and hanged without trial (A4, A10, A26).

Marshall was hanged by eight masked, armed men with others assisting, or by a 'party of citizens', who took him by force over a guard's or the sheriff's custody (A4, A10), and the Virginia Chronicle describes it as the work of a Vigilance Committee punishing a murder (A26). The papers give no race for Marshall, so whether this was anti-Black violence is not shown.

The wire dispatch, the Esmeralda Herald correspondent and the Virginia Chronicle's informant agree that Marshall was seized and hanged at Belleville for McCann's killing (A4, A10, A26), though they differ on custody, date and site.

accounts.label: Belleville wire dispatch (Dec. 10)
accounts.gist: Marshall was jailed after the killing; that morning, as the sheriff started with him for Aurora, citizens rushed the sheriff and posse, took Marshall and hanged him on the outskirts of town.

accounts.label: Esmeralda Herald correspondent
accounts.gist: The ironed prisoner was held in a room by guard Longabaugh; at about 4 A.M. eight masked, armed men took him and hanged him from a frame behind Farrington's blacksmith shop, helped by others outside, while the sheriff declined to resist.

accounts.label: Virginia Chronicle, from C. Raphael
accounts.gist: On a teamster's information, eight Vigilance Committee members took Marshall from his room at the Belleville Hotel at 3 A.M. Thursday and hanged him near the principal blacksmith shop; the story that he was taken from the sheriff was called incorrect.

framing.detail: Eastern and Midwestern papers ran the San Francisco wire under headlines such as 'LYNCHING A MURDERER' and 'A Murderer Lynched', calling Marshall 'a noted desperado' who killed 'an inoffensive old man'.
The Virginia Chronicle account, reprinted in Los Angeles, ran under 'THE LYNCHING APPROVED' and called the lynchers 'well-known, respectable citizens'.
The Esmeralda Herald letter, headed 'THE BELLEVILLE TRAGEDY' in Gold Hill and 'LYNCH LAW.' in Eureka, gave a detailed narrative without comment on the lynchers.
